column4: The section's source root رءي frames 89:6 as making the listener witness what the Lord did; this repeats the same question and wording for the people of the Elephant, making an earlier event present to the reader.
The section's source dictionary form المِرْصاد (root ر ص د) names a watchpoint; this ayah calls Hell مرصادًا, turning the hidden waiting place into the destination that receives the travelers.
The section's source root ر ص د gives المِرْصاد as a place where a watcher waits; the command to sit for the treaty-breakers at every مَرْصَد stages a human ambush on a route.

The section's source dictionary form المِرْصاد is a road-side watchpoint; Iblis says he will sit on God's straight صِرَاط to obstruct its travelers, reversing the Lord's unseen watch into a declared hostile one.

The section's source dictionary form المِرْصاد is where a watcher waits along a road; Shuʿayb forbids sitting at every صِرَاط to threaten passers and turn them aside, exposing the human version of the ambush.

The section names the root ر ص د and a serpent called رَصيد that waits for passers; the jinn find a شِهَابًا رَصَدًا waiting in the sky for anyone who tries to listen, a corresponding ambush from above.

The section's source root ر ص د names the watchers around a passage; here guards are placed before and behind God's messenger to protect what is revealed, making the watch protective rather than punitive.
The section says the unseen watcher waits where everyone must pass; this verse places a ready observer beside every utterance, extending the image from a road to what a person says.
The section's waiting watcher makes passage inescapable; this verse says every soul has a keeper over it, applying that oversight to each person.
The section develops the watcher's presence at a passage; this verse says keepers are appointed over people, a direct parallel in the scene of unseen oversight.
The section's watcher observes those who pass; as a continuation of 82:10, this ayah identifies the keepers as noble recorders, specifying what their watch does.
The section's watcher is present before the traveler knows it; continuing 82:10–11, this ayah says the recorders know what people do, giving the watch its content.
The section pictures the Lord waiting at the point every traveler must cross; this ayah describes Him as قائم over every soul for what it earns, making the watch continual and personal.
The section's watcher sees the passer before the passer sees him; this ayah says God knows the stealthy glance of the eyes and what breasts conceal, including what the observed person tries to hide.
The section links seeing (source root رءي) with transgression in the lands; here the Prophet's sight neither swerves nor exceeds its limit, a precise reversal of the transgressors' overstepping.
The section connects people who crossed limits in the lands with a human judging himself by what he has; this ayah says the human transgresses (يَطْغَى), giving that overreach an inward cause.
The section says the human looks at his own condition and reads abundance as honor; this ayah locates the error in seeing oneself as self-sufficient (رَآهُ اسْتَغْنَىٰ).

The section's human calls abundance proof of honor; this ayah has a person say, after receiving favor, “I was given it because of knowledge,” then calls the favor a trial (فِتْنَة), exposing the same misreading.

The section links excess provision with transgression in the lands; this ayah says that if God expanded provision to all servants they would البَغْيَ in the earth, while measured provision is sent as He wills, explaining the boundary behind the image.

The section describes plenty and scarcity as tests (ابتلاه); this ayah states directly that God tests people with evil and good (نَبْلُوكُم بِالشَّرِّ وَالْخَيْرِ فِتْنَةً), so neither condition by itself means honor or humiliation.
The section's human reads wealth as proof of being honored; this ayah asks whether provision of wealth and children is what the people think it is, opening a direct challenge to that reading.

The section presents wealth as a test misread as honor; this ayah rejects the assumption that God is hastening good to people by giving them wealth and children, marking provision as no guarantee of favor.
The section's person judges himself honored by abundance; these leaders say they have more wealth and children and therefore will not be punished, making that same inference explicit.
The section's human reads provision as rank; this ayah says God extends and measures provision as He wills, while most people do not know, correcting the inference.
The section shows wealth being mistaken for honor; this ayah says neither wealth nor children bring people nearer to God, except faith and right action, reversing the measure of status.

The section's human takes provision as a personal verdict; this ayah says God apportions livelihood and raises some above others in degrees, so material differences are assigned provision, not proof of moral worth.

The section contrasts the human's claim of honor with restricted provision; this ayah says the Lord extends or measures provision for whom He wills and is seeing of His servants, placing both conditions under a watchful giver.
The section's human equates plenty with honor; this ayah says God extends and measures provision, then adds that people rejoice in worldly life although its enjoyment is small beside the Hereafter.
The section's person looks at his provision and draws a verdict about himself; this ayah asks whether people see that God extends and measures provision, naming the allocation itself as a sign.
The section depicts a person judging honor by abundance; this ayah asks whether people know that God extends and measures provision for whom He wills, answering that judgment with divine choice.
The section's human sees abundance as honor; after Qarun's wealth ends in ruin, the onlookers recognize that God extends and measures provision for whom He wills, overturning their earlier envy.
The section calls the test through provision ابتلاء; this ayah explicitly calls wealth and children a فِتْنَة and points to the greater reward with God, clarifying that possession is a trial.
The section's human reads material ease as honor; this ayah calls wealth and children a trial (فِتْنَة) and says the great reward is with God.

The section shows a person mistaking worldly provision for honor; this ayah says one who desires the immediate life may receive it, but ends by warning of Hell, so immediate abundance does not certify divine approval.
The section's human reads ease as honor; this ayah warns disbelievers not to think that respite is good for them, since it only increases their sin, reversing the apparent meaning of worldly ease.
The section's human counts wealth as honor; this ayah tells the Prophet not to be impressed by disbelievers' wealth and children, which become a means of punishment for them.
The section's human claims that abundance means honor; Qarun says he received his wealth because of knowledge, repeating the self-crediting claim that 39:49 also exposes.

The section makes the human's gaze on abundance the subject; Qarun goes out in adornment, and those who desire worldly life wish for what he was given, showing how visible wealth teaches the wrong lesson.
The section describes abundance mistaken for honor; the people of knowledge answer Qarun's admirers that God's reward is better for those who believe and do right, setting a different measure.
The section's watcher and punishment make the apparent security of the powerful unstable; the earth swallows Qarun and his house, ending the display of wealth without a rescuer.
The section's human calls himself honored when provision is ample; the owner of the two gardens says he has more wealth and followers than his companion, voicing the same verdict from possessions.

The section's wealthy person mistakes present ease for honor; the garden owner assumes that if returned to his Lord he will receive something better, carrying the same worldly measure into the Hereafter.

The section's human reads a prosperous condition as honor; after his garden is ruined, its owner turns his hands over what he spent and recognizes the loss, a reversal of confidence in lasting provision.

The section's human reads ample provision as honor; God's answer to Abraham grants even the disbeliever brief enjoyment before driving him to the punishment of the Fire, separating provision from approval.

The section says travelers learn of the watcher only when the blow falls; this ayah asks whether a town can feel secure from punishment arriving at night while its people sleep, matching the unseen night strike.

The section's night traveler cannot see the waiting watcher; this neighboring warning asks whether people feel secure from punishment in daylight while they play, showing that no hour makes the passage safe.
The section's Lord waits at the point people must pass; this ayah asks whether people feel secure from God's plan and denies that security, stating the inward mistake behind missing the watcher.
The section's watcher waits where the traveler cannot avoid passing; this ayah asks whether plotters feel safe from being swallowed by the earth or struck from where they do not perceive.
The section's watcher does not need to pursue a traveler; this ayah says God may seize plotters while they go about and they cannot escape, making ordinary movement no protection.
The section says people discover the watcher at the blow; this ayah says punishment will come suddenly while they are unaware, despite their demand that it be hastened.
The section's fixed watchpoint makes the travelers' route lead into judgment; this ayah says Hell will encompass the disbelievers, completing the warning of sudden punishment in 29:53.

The section's dictionary note describes a serpent striking from above; this ayah depicts punishment covering people from above and from beneath their feet, turning the hidden strike into an inescapable enclosure.

The section's source dictionary connects the blow to a serpent dropping on its target from above; this ayah names punishment from above or beneath the feet, making the vertical attack an explicit divine threat.
The section links the watcher root ر ص د to a flame lying in wait in the sky; this ayah says the sky is guarded from every accursed devil, setting up the same celestial watch.
The section says a jinn who listens finds a flame lying in wait; this ayah says a devil who snatches a hearing is pursued by a clear flame, specifying the same interception.
The section's sky contains a watcher flame for a listener; this ayah says devils cannot listen to the highest assembly and are pelted from every side, giving the watch its purpose.
The section describes a flame waiting for the one who tries to listen; this ayah says the devils are driven away and face lasting punishment, continuing that intercepted passage.
The section's jinn meets a waiting flame while listening; this ayah allows only a thief who snatches a fragment of hearing, then says a piercing flame pursues him.
The section's image of a flame watching the sky is stated here as lamps made missiles for devils, a second formulation of the same guarded heaven.

The section shows the Lord's act on ʿĀd and Thamud and develops the path as a site of obstruction; this ayah says their dwellings remain visible, while Satan made their deeds pleasing and turned them from the path despite their perception.

The section invites the reader to see what happened to earlier peoples; this passage names the people of al-Ḥijr, who denied the messengers, locating another ruined community on the route through the land.
The section makes the reader an observer of a people's fate; this ayah says the people of al-Ḥijr were given signs yet turned away, connecting sight to failure to take warning.
The section's Thamud cut through rock in the valley; this ayah says the people of al-Ḥijr carved secure homes into the mountains, developing the same rock-cut habitation.
The section places the blow before it names the watchpoint; this ayah says a cry seized the people of al-Ḥijr in the morning, making the sudden punishment visible.
The section recalls the works of the people who crossed the land; this ayah says what they had earned did not avail them when the punishment came, reversing confidence in their built homes.
The section recalls peoples who crossed lands and exceeded their limits; this ayah says Thamud settled the plains and carved homes from mountains, then warns them not to spread corruption there.
The section asks the reader to see what God did to a people; this ayah says the cry seized the wrongdoers of Thamud and left them fallen in their homes, a sudden end in the very land they inhabited.
The section says Thamud cut through rock in a valley; this ayah describes them carving homes from mountains with skill, an explicit parallel to the rock-cut scene.
The section names the people who transgressed in the lands; this ayah says the extravagant corrupters do not reform the earth, giving the root's overstepping a social consequence.
The section names Thamud among those who transgressed; this ayah says Thamud denied in their rebellious excess (بِطَغْوَاهَا), making the same transgression the cause of their fate.
The section's watcher stands over travelers who cross a boundary; here the most wretched man rises to kill the she-camel after the warning, a boundary-breaking act before the punishment.
The section develops an unseen watch and the blow that follows; Salih warns them not to harm God's she-camel or prevent her drink, a concrete limit they are about to cross.
The section places a blow on transgressors before naming the watchpoint; this ayah says they hamstrung the camel and their Lord crushed them for their sin, connecting the broken limit to punishment.
The section's punishment leaves the powerful unable to escape the watcher; this ayah ends by saying God has no fear of the consequence, placing the human transgressors' exposure against divine power.
The section places ʿĀd and Thamud before the reader as witnessed peoples; this ayah names both as deniers of the striking calamity, directly recalling the same two communities.
The section asks the reader to see what was done to ʿĀd and Thamud; this ayah says Thamud were destroyed by the overpowering blast, giving the event its force.
The section recalls the fate of ʿĀd; this ayah says ʿĀd were destroyed by a furious, violent wind, another account of what the observer is asked to see.
The section's punishment descends on a people who overstepped; this ayah describes the wind sent against ʿĀd for seven nights and eight days, exposing them as fallen trunks.
The section makes the destroyed people an object of sight; this ayah asks whether any remnant of them can be seen after the wind, closing the visual account of ʿĀd.
The section also names Pharaoh among the peoples exposed to judgment; this ayah groups Pharaoh and the overturned towns among those who committed error.
The section names transgression in the lands before the punishment; this ayah says they disobeyed their Lord's messenger, so He seized them with an overwhelming seizure.
The section asks the listener to see what the Lord did to ʿĀd; this ayah repeats that ʿĀd denied and asks how severe the punishment and warning were.
The section presents the blow falling on an overreaching people; this ayah describes the destructive wind sent against ʿĀd on an ill-fated day.
The section's punished travelers are made to witness the force of the strike; this ayah says the wind tore people away as though they were uprooted palm trunks.
The section presents the punishment as what an observer must recognize; this ayah again asks how severe the punishment and warning were for ʿĀd.
The section names ʿĀd among those who transgressed in the lands; this ayah says they arrogantly claimed none was stronger than them, though their Creator was stronger.
The section asks the reader to witness God's act against ʿĀd; this ayah says a furious wind brought them humiliating punishment in worldly life, while the Hereafter's punishment is more humiliating.
The section's image turns on the difference between seeing and taking heed; this ayah says Thamud were shown guidance but chose blindness, then were seized by a humiliating blast.

The section places the exposed wrongdoers beside the people who heed warning; this ayah says God saved those who believed and were mindful, marking the boundary between the punished and the protected.

The section's source root س ر ي describes people traveling at night; Moses is commanded to take the Children of Israel by night (فَأَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي), and God opens a dry path through the sea for them.
The section's night travelers must pass through a route they do not control; as the continuation of 20:77, Pharaoh follows them into the sea and is overwhelmed, reversing who survives the crossing.
The section's source root س ر ي names a company moving by night; Lot is told to take his family out in part of the night, with his wife excepted from the escape.
The section's source root س ر ي describes night travel; Lot is commanded to travel with his family during part of the night and keep moving as instructed.
The section's source root س ر ي names those who travel at night; Moses receives the same command to take God's servants by night before Pharaoh pursues them.
The section's source root س ر ي describes a group moving at night; Moses is again told to travel by night with God's servants, making the night route a repeated escape scene.
The section's source root س ر ي concerns night travel; this ayah says God carried His servant by night, a guided journey rather than the threatened escape of Lot and Moses.

The section makes ruined peoples an object for the reader's sight; this ayah tells people to travel the earth and look at how the deniers ended, turning movement through lands into witnessing their fate.
The section joins country-crossing with observing what befell earlier peoples; this ayah directly commands travel through the earth and look at the end of the deniers.
The section shows the listener the fate of earlier peoples; this ayah asks whether people traveled through the land to see how those before ended, then contrasts the lasting home of the Hereafter.
The section recalls the outcome of transgressors; this ayah sends people to travel the land and see the end of those who denied the messengers.
The section's travelers cross lands marked by the ruins of former peoples; this ayah depicts destroyed townships with collapsed roofs, abandoned wells, and tall palaces left empty.
The section's source root رءي means seeing with eye or insight; this ayah asks people to travel and reason, then says blindness is in hearts rather than eyes, making observation a test of perception.
The section makes the reader witness the end of overreaching peoples; this ayah tells people to travel the land and see the end of the guilty.
The section recalls peoples who crossed lands and exceeded limits; this ayah asks people to travel and see the end of predecessors, noting their greater strength and the messengers' clear signs.
The section makes past peoples' fate visible; this ayah commands travel through the earth and observe the end of those before, most of whom associated partners with God.
The section's observer is asked to see what happened to old peoples; this ayah asks whether people traveled and saw the end of those before them, who were stronger yet could not escape God.
The section links travel through countries to punishment of transgressors; this ayah asks people to travel and see that earlier, stronger peoples were seized for their sins.
The section makes ruined peoples evidence for the passing traveler; this ayah repeats the command to travel and see how earlier, stronger generations ended.
The section asks its listener to witness the outcome of earlier peoples; this ayah asks whether people traveled the land and saw how God destroyed those before them.
The section shifts from looking at earlier peoples to looking at oneself; this ayah tells each person to read his own record, making the observed person his own reckoner.
The section turns the gaze inward after showing a people's fate; this ayah says each person's record is fixed to him and will be brought forth on Judgment Day, preparing the self-reading of 17:14.
The section says the human looks at his own condition; this ayah calls the human a witness against himself, even if he offers excuses.
The section contrasts eyes that see with the hidden watcher's knowledge; this ayah says hearing, eyes, and skins testify when people reach the Fire, making their own faculties witnesses.
The section moves from observing others to one's own state; this ayah says mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what people did.
The section's watcher records what passes before him; this ayah says whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, making even the smallest deed visible.
The section's unseen observer does not miss the passer; this ayah says whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, completing the reckoning of 99:7.
The section's human may not notice the watcher until judgment; this ayah says every soul arrives with a driver and a witness, staging the final passage under observation.
The section's human eye looks outward while the Lord watches the traveler; this ayah says eyes cannot encompass Him but He encompasses all eyes, setting the watcher beyond human sight.

The section distinguishes looking with the eye from seeing with insight; this ayah says the veil is removed and sight is sharp on that day, reversing the earlier failure to recognize what was happening.

The section's people are made to look at what happened to them; this ayah says hearing and eyes did not help the people of ʿĀd because they denied God's signs, showing that seeing alone is no protection.
The section defines seeing as eye or insight; this ayah says some have eyes but do not see, alongside hearts that do not understand, naming the failure of perception behind the ruined peoples.
The section's human makes a verdict from his worldly condition; this ayah asks whether he thinks no one can overpower him, beginning a portrait of false self-security.
The section's human sees wealth as honor; this ayah has him boast that he spent abundant wealth, turning possession into self-display.
The section's watcher is unseen until the traveler is struck; this ayah asks whether the boastful human thinks no one sees him, exposing the same false security.
The section's present human repeats an old misreading of abundance; this continuation of 39:49 says earlier people made the same claim and were struck by the consequences of what they earned.
The section's human calls a favor honor; following the claim in 39:49–50, this ayah says the evil they earned struck them, reversing their confidence in the favor.
The section's human reads wealth as lasting honor; the garden owner enters his garden while wronging himself and says he does not think it will ever perish, showing how abundance conceals its limit.

The section's man judges himself by wealth; his companion asks why he did not acknowledge God upon entering the garden, then notes his own lesser wealth and children, exposing the comparison by possessions.

The section's abundant person takes his condition as honor; the companion says God may give him something better than the garden, then turn the garden into barren ground, exposing provision's impermanence.
The section's powerful people cannot outrun the watchpoint; after the garden is ruined, its owner has no group to help him against God.
The section's human attributes honor to his own abundance; this ayah says true protection and authority belong to God, the right in whom to hope.
The section shows the human assessing himself through wealth; Qarun is given treasures so heavy that their keys burden a group of strong men, making his material standing visible.

The section's source dictionary links مِثَال (image) with seeing; this ayah develops a visible parable of light, a niche, glass, and a brilliant star, showing the Qur'an's image-language as a means of perception.
The section's source dictionary gives مَثَل the secondary sense of lesson; this ayah says the Qur'an sets out every kind of example for people so they may remember.
The section's source dictionary links مَثَل with an instructive example; this ayah says such parables are set forth for people, though only those who know understand them.
The section's source dictionary gives مَثَل the sense of lesson; this ayah says the destroyed people were made a precedent and an example for those who came later, like the peoples shown in 89.

The section's source dictionary joins image (تمثال) and lesson (مثل); this ayah says that if the Qur'an were sent on a mountain, one would see it humbled and split from fear, then calls such comparisons a means to reflect.

The section presents 9:5's ambush command against treaty-breakers; this preceding ayah exempts those who honored their treaties and orders the pact to be fulfilled, defining the boundary of the waiting punishment.
